items.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, section 226: Misleading actions
items.why: The test a public AI claim is judged by where consumers are the audience: false or misleading information, or an overall presentation likely to deceive even if the information is true. In force 6 April 2025 (S.I. 2025/272). Covers consumers only (s.225(3)).
items.quote: an overall presentation which is likely to deceive the average consumer about a matter relating to a product, a trader or any other matter

items.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, section 182: Final infringement notice
items.why: The CMA decides the breach itself and may impose a penalty not exceeding £300,000 or, if higher, 10% of turnover (s.182(6)); it may also require a corrective statement to be published (s.182(8)).
items.quote: a fixed amount not exceeding £300,000 or, if higher, 10% of the total value of the turnover (if any) of the respondent

items.title: Regulating the Illusion of Intelligence in Ads
items.locator: Section 'Human Advice vs Machine Learning' (CAP News, 27 Aug 2026)
items.why: Source of the quotation. Advice on adverts for AI assistants: objective capability claims must be substantiated. It is advice from the self-regulatory body, not law, and the Code covers the advert, not the product.
items.quote: Hold evidence to back up any objective claims about what your product can do

items.title: 'AI' as a Marketing Term: A Quantitative Review of Usage in UK Advertising
items.why: Source of the figure (around 16,000 adverts, p.3; 68% business-to-business, p.4). CAP advice on p.5: do not falsely claim a product uses AI, exaggerate what it can do, or claim it beats a non-AI product without good evidence.
items.quote: we identified around 16k unique relevant ads between July and September 2024

items.title: The Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008, regulation 3
items.why: The rule for claims made to business buyers, where most AI advertising sits: advertising that deceives traders and is likely to affect their economic behaviour is prohibited, including on fitness for purpose and results to be expected.
items.quote: deceives or is likely to deceive the traders to whom it is addressed or whom it reaches

items.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, Schedule 10A: Liability of issuers in connection with published information
items.why: Investor-facing claims: an issuer of securities admitted to trading is liable for an untrue or misleading published statement only if a person discharging managerial responsibilities knew it was so or was reckless (para 3(2)), and the investor reasonably relied on it (para 3(4)).
items.quote: knew the statement to be untrue or misleading or was reckless as to whether it was untrue or misleading

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 463: Liability for false or misleading statements in reports and statements
items.quote: he knew the statement to be untrue or misleading or was reckless as to whether it was untrue or misleading
items.why: Claims in the annual report: a director must compensate the company for loss caused by an untrue or misleading statement in the strategic report, directors' report, remuneration report or corporate governance statement, if the director knew or was reckless. Liability is to the company only (s.463(4)); it does not give investors or customers a claim.

items.title: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, section 199: Failure to prevent fraud
items.locator: s.199(1), (4); commencement note I2; fraud offences listed in Schedule 13
items.quote: such prevention procedures as it was reasonable in all the circumstances to expect the body to have in place
items.why: Since 1 September 2025 (S.I. 2025/349) a large organisation commits an offence if an employee or other associate commits a listed fraud offence intending to benefit it, unless it had reasonable prevention procedures. Reasonable prevention procedures are the defence, which gives checks on claims before publication legal weight. Applies to large organisations only and needs an underlying fraud offence (dishonesty); an honest overstatement is not caught.

items.title: Unfair commercial practices (CMA207)
items.locator: Chapter 'Misleading actions', 'Misleading action type 2: Overall deceptive presentation' and its example
items.quote: they will have been deceived by the overall presentation and misled
items.why: The enforcing regulator's guidance on the test an AI claim to consumers must pass, with worked examples of statements that are each factually correct yet mislead as a whole. General consumer law: the guidance does not mention AI. The date is the page's 'updated' date.

items.title: UK Code of Non-broadcast Advertising and Direct & Promotional Marketing (CAP Code), Section 3: Misleading advertising
items.quote: marketers must hold documentary evidence to prove claims that consumers are likely to regard as objective
items.why: The rule behind the advertising regulator's advice on AI products: evidence must be held before the advert is published, and claims may be judged misleading without it. A self-regulatory code enforced by the ASA, not law; it covers advertising, not annual reports or bids. The page shows no date, so the year is the year read.

items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.locator: Section 4, Principles M and N (PDF p.13); Provision 25 on the audit committee's review
items.quote: The board should present a fair, balanced and understandable assessment of the company's position and prospects.
items.why: The standard a listed company's annual report is held to, with the board required to satisfy itself on the integrity of narrative as well as financial statements. Applies to listed companies on a comply or explain basis; it does not mention AI. Dated January 2024 on the document.

items.title: Alan Bates and Others v Post Office Limited, Judgment (No.6) 'Horizon Issues' [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB)
items.publisher: High Court of Justice, Queen's Bench Division (Courts and Tribunals Judiciary)
items.quote: were factually untrue in at least one highly important respect
items.why: A UK court finding on exactly this gap: the Post Office had said publicly that its Horizon system was robust; the judge found earlier public statements factually untrue and that the older system was not robust. Not an AI system and not a ruling on advertising or securities law; cited as an official finding on public claims about a computer system that its owner could not support.

items.title: SEC Charges Two Investment Advisers with Making False and Misleading Statements About Their Use of Artificial Intelligence (press release 2024-36)
items.quote: Investment advisers should not mislead the public by saying they are using an AI model when they are not.
items.why: International comparator: a US securities enforcement action the regulator itself described as 'AI washing'. Two advisers settled and paid $400,000 in total civil penalties for claims about AI they were not using. A US press release about settled charges under US law; no equivalent UK action was found in this pass.

items.title: FTC Announces Crackdown on Deceptive AI Claims and Schemes (Operation AI Comply)
items.quote: there is no AI exemption from the laws on the books
items.why: International comparator on the consumer side: five enforcement actions in one sweep, including a company claiming to sell 'AI Lawyer' services. Shows a regulator applying ordinary deception law to AI claims, as UK law would. US law and US cases; a press release, not a judgment.

items.title: Public Statement on the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the provision of retail investment services (ESMA35-335435667-5924)
items.quote: they ensure that such information is presented in a clear, fair and not misleading manner
items.why: The EU securities regulator's expectation that what investment firms tell clients about their use of AI must be clear, fair and not misleading. EU guidance under MiFID II for investment firms; not UK, and limited to retail investment services.

items.title: Trusted third-party AI assurance roadmap
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Introduction and the section on professionalisation (auditing)
items.quote: Auditing has a particularly important role to play in independently verifying the trustworthiness of AI systems.
items.why: Government's account of the independent assurance the top level of this criterion calls for, and of how immature that market is. A policy roadmap, not a standard: it describes no scheme for assuring an organisation's public AI claims and requires nothing of companies.

items.title: The Fallacy of AI Functionality
items.publisher: Inioluwa Deborah Raji, I. Elizabeth Kumar, Aaron Horowitz and Andrew D. Selbst (arXiv; published in FAccT 2022)
items.quote: They can be constructed haphazardly, deployed indiscriminately, and promoted deceptively.
items.why: Research on the gap this criterion measures: a taxonomy, built from case studies, of deployed AI systems that did not do what was claimed for them. Authors' repository copy (v2, 1 July 2022) of a peer-reviewed conference paper; case studies, not a measured rate.

items.title: Are Companies Taking AI Risks Seriously? A Systematic Analysis of Companies' AI Risk Disclosures in SEC 10-K forms
items.publisher: Lucas G. Uberti-Bona Marin, Bram Rijsbosch, Gerasimos Spanakis and Konrad Kollnig (arXiv preprint; to appear in the ECML PKDD SoGood workshop proceedings)
items.quote: many disclosures remain generic or lack details on mitigation strategies
items.why: Evidence on what companies actually say about AI in annual filings: over 30,000 filings from more than 7,000 companies; mentions of AI risk rose from 4% in 2020 to over 43% in 2024, but many were generic. US filings only; workshop paper, preprint.

items.title: AI Washing and the Erosion of Digital Legitimacy: A Socio-Technical Perspective on Responsible Artificial Intelligence in Business
items.quote: marketing and branding, technical capability inflation, strategic signaling, and governance-based washing
items.why: A typology of overstated AI claims that separates claims about capability from claims about governance, the distinction the brief draws. Single-author preprint marked as under review, not peer reviewed; conceptual, with no data.
